newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean state firm plans land project in North.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean state firm plans land project in North.

text.p: A South Korean state company has agreed in principle to develop an industrial estate in North Korea but Seoul said on Wednesday the project depended on progress in relations between the two rival states.
The Korea Land Corp said it signed a letter of intent in Beijing on Sunday with the North's Committee for Promotion of External Economic Cooperation.

The project, covering 6.6 million square metres (71 million square feet), is within the Rajin-Sonbong area, designated by cash-strapped Pyongyang as a free economic and trade zone to help encourage foreign investment.
A Korea Land Corp official said the project would involve hundreds of millions of dollars but its exact cost was unknown.
"The project, if implemented, will encourage South Korean and foreign companies to invest in the Rajin-Sonbong area," he said.
"We have agreed with North Korean officials to continue working-level negotiations but we need approval from the government to go ahead with the project."
A Unification Ministry statement said the letter of intent was not legally binding and that the project had "some problems and requires serious review at this stage".
"The government plans to handle this issue carefully in connection with progress in South-North relations," it said.

A ministry official said any major economic cooperation with North Korea would depend on Pyongyang's willingness to have a dialogue with the South and to take steps to reduce tensions on the Korean peninsula.

On Tuesday, senior South Korean diplomats left New York after a frustrating series of talks with North Koreans that failed to persuade Pyongyang to join proposed peace talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China.
But Seoul officials said they were hopeful the North would eventually say yes to the talks aimed at achieving a lasting peace to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

In negotiations in New York between representatives of the United States and two Koreas, the North agreed in principle to join the talks but demanded promises be made for large-scale food aid first, Seoul officials said.
The United States and South Korea, which jointly proposed the peace talks, maintain that substantial food aid can only be discussed during the four-way talks.
Diplomats in Seoul said statements by Hwang Jang-yop, the most senior North Korean official to defect from the famine-threatened North, could also affect relations between the two Koreas.

Hwang, chief architect of Pyongyang's guiding ideology of "juche", or self-reliance, arrived in Seoul on Sunday and warned that the North did not want peace with the South and was bent on preparing for a new war on the peninsula.
